docs.text:
Metanno brings data exploration and annotation into JupyterLab. Open data prepared in Python, inspect it through tables, text and image views, and save an editable dataset. Move between your notebook and the viewer as you select data, add predictions and review annotations.

Metanno supplies the visualization and annotation components. Pret connects them to shared Python data and saves your work. You can also compose these components directly in notebook outputs or standalone Pret applications.

Who is it for? Research groups, clinical NLP and biomedical teams, data labeling squads, and anyone who wants custom and interactive annotation tools without wrestling with JavaScript.

docs.title: Choose a starting point
docs.text:
• Install Metanno in the Jupyter server and Python environments you use
  • Annotate a table in five minutes, without any configuration
  • Annotate a corpus: select notes in a database, pre-annotate them with EDS-NLP and review them
  • Customize the interface of your annotators, inside or outside JupyterLab

docs.title: Open data prepared in Python
docs.text:
from metanno import view_opener
from pret import DataFrame, create_store

store = create_store({"notes": DataFrame([{"id": 1, "text": "Example"}])}, sync=True)
view_opener(store)

Click Open with Metanno to open the table in a tab. This is an unsaved preview. Follow Annotate a table to make an editable copy, read edits back into Python and reopen the saved file. It needs no source configuration or custom interface code.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
In addition to the Pret component suite, Metanno provides components for common annotation views:

  • AnnotatedText: display text with highlighted, nestable spans
  • AnnotatedImage: draw shapes (boxes, polygons, etc.) over images
  • Table: an editable, filterable spreadsheet-style grid for inspecting and editing annotations

Compose them in notebook outputs, standalone Pret apps, or views opened in the JupyterLab viewer. Several views of the same annotations stay in sync, since they share the same Store.

docs.title: Why another annotation software?
docs.text:
Tool choice shapes both the annotation scheme and the workflow. In many out-of-the-box tools, tasks like annotating implicit or document-level entities, working across multiple documents at once, or coordinating multiple views can be difficult or unsupported. There are many available solutions (see Neves et al.). However, most of these are either proprietary, poorly adapted to document or multi-document annotation, require a complex installation that is not compatible with existing strict remote computing environments, or are difficult to customize.

Metanno takes a different approach: a modular, Python-first framework that adapts to your schema and to your annotation process, instead of forcing you into fixed layers or rigid UIs. In JupyterLab, it needs no additional port and no separate server process.

docs.title: Compose your own components
docs.text:
For a table and text view connected to saved rows, start with Review entities. The example below shows the lower-level components using a small list of dictionaries. This path is useful when you want to write the interaction callbacks yourself.

Below is a small example that lets you annotate text spans and view them in a synchronized table. Select spans to add them; hold Shift (also labeled Maj on some keyboards) while selecting to delete overlapping spans.

Show code 
from pret import component, create_store, use_store_snapshot, use_event_callback
from metanno import AnnotatedText

state = create_store(
    [
        {"text": "soir", "begin": 3, "end": 7, "id": "s-3-7", "label": "ENT"},
        {"text": "Charlie", "begin": 59, "end": 66, "id": "s-59-66", "label": "ENT"},
    ]
)

text = (
    "Le soir, après avoir mangé sa soupe aux choux noyée "
    "d’eau, Charlie allait toujours dans la chambre de ses "
    "quatre grands-parents pour écouter leurs histoires, "
    "et pour leur souhaiter bonne nuit.\n"
    "Chacun d’eux avait plus de quatre-vingt-dix ans. Ils "
    "étaient fripés comme des pruneaux secs, ossus comme "
    "des squelettes et, toute la journée, jusqu’à l’apparition "
    "de Charlie, ils se pelotonnaient dans leur lit, deux de "
    "chaque côté, coiffés de bonnets de nuit qui leur tenaient "
    "chaud, passant le temps à ne rien faire."
)


@component
def App():
    view_state = use_store_snapshot(state)

    @use_event_callback
    def on_select(spans, mod_keys):
        if "Shift" in mod_keys:
            # Delete overlapped spans if the user holds Shift
            state[:] = [
                x
                for x in state
                if any(
                    (s["begin"] >= x["end"] or s["end"] <= x["begin"]) for s in spans
                )
            ]
        else:
            state.extend(
                [
                    {
                        **s,
                        "id": f"s-{s['begin']}-{s['end']}",
                        "text": text[s["begin"] : s["end"]],
                        "label": "ENT",
                    }
                    for s in spans
                ]
            )

    return AnnotatedText(
        text=text,
        spans=view_state,
        annotation_styles={"ENT": {"color": "lightblue"}},
        on_mouse_select=on_select,
    )


App()

The annotations are reflected in the table below. Both views stay in sync because they share the same state (state).

Show code 
# ↑ Complete the code above with the following snippet ↑
from pret import component, use_store_snapshot, use_event_callback
from metanno import Table

columns = [
    {"key": "id", "kind": "text", "name": "id", "filterable": True},
    {"key": "begin", "kind": "text", "name": "begin", "filterable": True},
    {"key": "end", "kind": "text", "name": "end", "filterable": True},
    {"key": "text", "kind": "text", "name": "text", "filterable": True},
    {"key": "label", "kind": "text", "name": "label", "filterable": True,
        "editable": True, "choices": ["ENT", "OTHER"]},
]


@component
def MyTable():
    @use_event_callback
    def on_cell_change(row_idx, col, new_value):
        view_state[row_idx][col] = new_value

    for x in state:
        x.setdefault("label", "ENT")  # Ensure all rows have a label

    view_state = use_store_snapshot(state)
    return Table(
        rows=view_state,
        columns=columns,
        auto_filter=True,
        on_cell_change=on_cell_change,
    )


MyTable()

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Metanno runs in JupyterLab 3 or 4, with Python 3.10 or later. For a first try, install it in the Python environment that runs JupyterLab:

pip install metanno
python -m metanno.viewer.explorer_kernel --install

The second command registers the metanno-explorer kernel, which reads your databases for the Metanno sidebar. Refresh JupyterLab: the Metanno icon appears in the left sidebar, and you can start with Annotate a table.

docs.title: In a project
docs.text:
To keep Metanno with the other dependencies of your project, add it to your pyproject.toml or requirements.txt, then install them in a new environment:

pyproject.tomlrequirements.txt 
[project]
name = "my-annotation-project"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
"metanno>=2.0.0-beta.1",
"edsnlp>=0.21",  # used to pre-annotate the documents
]

mamba create -n annotation python=3.11 -y
mamba activate annotation
pip install .

metanno>=2.0.0-beta.1
edsnlp>=0.21  # used to pre-annotate the documents

mamba create -n annotation python=3.11 -y
mamba activate annotation
pip install -r requirements.txt

When JupyterLab runs in another environment, register this one as a notebook kernel, then select it in the top-right corner of your notebooks:

pip install ipykernel
python -m ipykernel install --user --name annotation

JupyterLab then needs the sidebar and tabs of Metanno, installed in this environment: run this command in it once, then refresh JupyterLab in your browser.

pret update-jupyter-config --apply

It links the front-end files of Metanno and Pret into your Jupyter data folder (~/.local/share/jupyter/labextensions), which JupyterLab reads whatever its own environment.

docs.title: Check your installation
docs.text:
Run this cell in a notebook:

from pret import component
from pret_joy import Button


@component
def SanityCheckApp():
    return Button("Metanno is installed ✅", sx={"m": 1})


SanityCheckApp()

A button appears below the cell when JupyterLab and your kernel are ready. Nothing shows up? Check that the kernel of the notebook is the environment where you installed Metanno: import sys; print(sys.executable) prints its path.

docs.title: Databases and the explorer kernel
docs.text:
The metanno-explorer kernel reads the databases listed in metanno.yaml, as shown in Browse a database. Install it, with the Ibis driver of each database, in the environment that can reach these databases:

pip install metanno 'ibis-framework[duckdb]'
python -m metanno.viewer.explorer_kernel --install

Install each driver through its Ibis extra, eg 'ibis-framework[pyspark]' for Spark, even when the driver itself comes from another package index: the extra also installs the packages Ibis needs to read its results.

Registering records the Python executable that ran the command, so this environment can differ from the ones of JupyterLab and of your notebooks, which do not need the explorer kernel to open notebook data.

The sidebar says the explorer kernel is missing

Run the registration command above in the intended environment, then click Retry in the sidebar. jupyter kernelspec list, run in the environment of JupyterLab, lists the kernels JupyterLab can find. When JupyterLab runs as another user or on another machine, its administrator must register the kernel there, with a Python executable available on that machine.

Open configuration still works while the kernel is missing, and notebook views still open in their own kernels.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text:
Metanno views are built from two kinds of blocks. The widgets of DataWidgetFactory are connected to a Store: they read its rows, save the edits and share the selected row with each other, and most views, like the ones of the tutorials, only use them. Under them, the components only display what they receive, and let you write what happens on each click or selection.

Block What it is DataWidgetFactory tables, texts, forms and PDFs connected to a Store, the usual way to build a view AnnotatedText a text with highlighted spans, reporting the text you select and the spans you click AnnotatedImage an image with boxes and shapes drawn on it, reporting the shapes you draw Table rows in an editable grid, reporting the cells you edit and select

Use the components directly when the factory widgets do not fit, for instance to decide yourself what a text selection adds. The front page shows a text and a table built this way. All these blocks are Pret components: they work in Metanno tabs, notebook outputs and web apps alike.

docs.title: AnnotatedImage
docs.text:
An interactive image viewer that supports drawing, selecting, and styling geometric shapes (polygons, rectangles, points...) as annotations.

Under the hood, we use Konva to render the image and its annotations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from pret import component, create_store, use_store_snapshot, use_event_callback
from metanno import AnnotatedImage
import time

# Reactive store holding the annotation list
img_state = create_store([
    {
        "id": "1",
        "type": "polygon",
        "points": [10, 10, 50, 20],
        "label": "OBJ",
        "style": "primary",
    }
])

# Style preset referenced from the annotation above
img_annotation_styles = {
    "primary": {
        "strokeColor": "red",
        "strokeWidth": 2,
        "fillColor": "rgba(255,0,0,0.5)",
        "labelPosition": "center",
        "align": "center",
        "verticalAlign": "top",
    },
    "secondary": {
        "strokeColor": "blue",
        "strokeWidth": 2,
        "fillColor": "#0000ff80",
        "textColor": "white",
    }
}

@component
def MyImage():
    tracked_state = use_store_snapshot(img_state)

    @use_event_callback
    def on_mouse_select(modkeys, shapes):
        # Toggle 'mouseSelected' flag
        for shp in shapes:
            img_state.append({
                "id": str(time.time()),
                "points": shp["points"],
                "label": "OBJ",
                "style": "primary",
            })

    @use_event_callback
    def on_click(shape_idx, modkeys):
        if shape_idx is None:
            img_state.clear()
        else:
            old_style = img_state[shape_idx].get("style", "primary")
            new_style = "secondary" if old_style == "primary" else "primary"
            img_state[shape_idx]["style"] = new_style

    return AnnotatedImage(
        image="https://picsum.photos/400/300",
        annotations=tracked_state,
        annotation_styles=img_annotation_styles,
        on_mouse_select=on_mouse_select,
        on_click=on_click,
    )

MyImage()

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION annotations

List of annotation objects drawn on top of the image. Each annotation must contain the geometric type and points fields (defining the shape) plus optional metadata such as:

  • id: Optional unique identifier.
  • label: Human-readable text shown next to the shape.
  • style: Key that looks up visual properties in annotation_styles.
  • selected / highlighted / mouseSelected: Booleans used by the component when rendering interaction state.

TYPE: Any

annotation_styles

Named style presets referenced by the style field of an annotation. Each preset may define properties such as stroke color, fill color, opacity, font size, and label alignment, using the following properties:

  • strokeColor (str): Color of the shape's stroke (e.g. "#ff0000").
  • strokeWidth (int): Width of the shape's stroke in pixels.
  • fillColor (str): Background color of the shape (e.g. "#0000ff80").
  • opacity (float): Opacity of the shape's fill (0.0 to 1.0).
  • shape (str): Shape type, e.g. "polygon", "rectangle", "circle", etc.
  • fontSize (int): Font size for the label text.
  • align ("left" | "center" | "right"): Horizontal alignment of the label text.
  • verticalAlign ("top" | "middle" | "bottom"): Vertical alignment of the label text.

TYPE: Any

image

Source URL or base-64 data URI of the image to annotate.

TYPE: str

mouse_selection

Temporary shapes being drawn by the user while the mouse button is held down. Supplied back to on_mouse_select when the gesture ends.

TYPE: Any

style

Inline CSS-compatible style overrides for the root element of the component.

TYPE: Any

handle

Optional imperative handle that the parent may call (empty for now).

TYPE: Any

key

React key for stable reconciliation.

TYPE: Union[str, int]

on_click

Invoked when the user clicks on an existing shape.

  • shape_id: Identifier of the clicked annotation
  • modkeys: List of pressed modifier keys (e.g. ["Shift"])

TYPE: Any

on_key_press

Invoked when the component has focus and the user presses a key.

  • key: The key name ("Escape", "Delete" …)
  • modkeys: Concurrently pressed modifier keys

TYPE: Any

on_mouse_enter_shape

Hover callbacks fired when the mouse pointer enters or leaves a shape.

TYPE: Any

on_mouse_select

Fired after the user completes a drag selection.

  • modkeys: Modifier keys pressed during selection
  • shapes: All shapes inside the lasso / rectangle

TYPE: Any

docs.title: AnnotatedText
docs.text: The AnnotatedText is a rich text viewer that supports span-level annotations, nested token highlights, and various user event callbacks.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from pret import (
    component,
    create_store,
    use_store_snapshot,
    use_event_callback,
    use_state,
)
from metanno import AnnotatedText
from pret_joy import Button, Box

txt = (
    "Metanno brings annotation components to Pret\n"
    "to build tailored annotation tools."
)

# One span covering the word “Metanno”
spans = create_store(
    [
        {
            "id": f"span-0-7",
            "start": 0,
            "end": 7,
            "label": "OBJ",
            "highlighted": False,
        }
    ]
)

txt_annotation_styles = create_store(
    {
        "OBJ": {
            "color": "red",
            "shape": "underline",
        }
    }
)


@component
def MyText():
    tracked_spans = use_store_snapshot(spans)
    tracked_styles = use_store_snapshot(txt_annotation_styles)

    @use_event_callback
    def handle_select(ranges, modkeys):
        for sp in ranges:
            spans.extend(
                [
                    {
                        "id": f"span-{sp['begin']}-{sp['end']}",
                        "start": sp["begin"],
                        "end": sp["end"],
                        "label": "OBJ",
                    }
                ]
            )

    def on_mouse_enter_span(span_id, modkeys):
        for i, sp in enumerate(spans):
            if sp["id"] == span_id:
                spans[i]["highlighted"] = True

    def on_mouse_leave_span(span_id, modkeys):
        for i, sp in enumerate(spans):
            if sp["id"] == span_id:
                spans[i]["highlighted"] = False

    def on_span_style_change():
        old_style = txt_annotation_styles["OBJ"]["shape"]
        new_style = "box" if old_style == "underline" else "underline"
        txt_annotation_styles["OBJ"]["shape"] = new_style

    return Box(
        Button("Change style", on_click=on_span_style_change),
        Button("Remove annotations", on_click=lambda: spans.clear()),
        AnnotatedText(
            text=txt,
            spans=tracked_spans,
            annotation_styles=tracked_styles,
            label_formatter=lambda span: f"{span['label']} ({span['end'] - span['start']} chars)",
            on_mouse_select=handle_select,
            on_mouse_enter_span=on_mouse_enter_span,
            on_mouse_leave_span=on_mouse_leave_span,
            style={"gridColumn": "1 / -1"},
            begin_key="start",  # Custom field names
        ),
        sx={
            "p": 1,
            "display": "grid",
            "gridTemplateColumns": "repeat(2, auto)",
            "gap": 1,
        },
    )


MyText()

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION text

Raw text content shown in the viewer.

TYPE: str

spans

Span-level annotations over text. Each span must include:

  • begin (or the value of begin_key): Begin character offset (inclusive).
  • end (or the value of end_key): End character offset (exclusive).

and may optionally include:

  • id (or the value of primary_key): Optional unique span identifier.
  • label (or the value of label_key): Category name displayed next to / above the span.
  • style (or the value of style_key): Key referencing annotation_styles.
  • selected (or the value of selected_key): styled as selected by the user.
  • highlighted (or the value of label_key): styled as highlighted by the user.

TYPE: List[Dict[str, Any]]

annotation_styles

Named style presets that control span background color, border, label placement, etc. Each style may define properties such as:

  • color (str): Color of the span. Will be overridden by backgroundColor and borderColor.
  • shape ("underline" | "box"): Visual style of the span.
  • backgroundColor (str): Background color of the span (e.g. "#0000ff80").
  • borderColor (str): Border color of the span (e.g. "#000000").
  • autoNestingLayout (bool): Whether to automatically nest overlapping spans, rather than rendering them on top of each other.

TYPE: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]]

mouse_selection

Current mouse drag selection expressed as character‐offset ranges. Passed to on_mouse_select when the action completes.

TYPE: List[Dict[str, int]]

style

CSS style overrides for the outer element.

TYPE: Dict[str, Any]

handle

Imperative handle for actions that can be performed on the component:

  • scroll_to_line(line_idx: int, behavior: "smooth" | "instant" | "auto"): Scrolls to the given line index.
  • scroll_to_span(span_id: str, behavior: "smooth" | "instant" | "auto"): Scrolls to the given span.
  • clear_current_mouse_selection(): Clears the current mouse selection.

TYPE: Dict[str, Any]

begin_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the begin character offset.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'begin'

end_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the end character offset.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'end'

primary_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the unique span identifier.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'id'

label_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the human-readable label.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'label'

label_formatter

Optional function used to compute each displayed span label from the full span dictionary. When provided, its return value is shown instead of the uppercased value from label_key.

TYPE: Optional[Callable[[Dict[str, Any]], str]] DEFAULT: None

style_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the style key. This key will be used to look up visual properties in annotation_styles. If no style field is provided for a span, the style key will default to label.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'style'

highlighted_key

Name of the field in spans that indicates whether the span is highlighted.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'highlighted'

highlighted

Identifiers of spans styled as highlighted by adding a class to their elements, without tokenizing the text again. Prefer it for fast changing highlights such as hovered spans.

TYPE: Optional[List[str]] DEFAULT: None

on_click_span

Called when the user clicks on a span.

  • span_id: Identifier of the clicked annotation
  • modkeys: Pressed modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[str, List[str]], None]

on_key_press

Called when a key is pressed with focus inside the component.

  • key: Key name
  • ranges: Current selection ranges
  • modkeys: Modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[str, List[Dict[str, int]], List[str]], None]

on_mouse_enter_span

Called when the mouse pointer enters a span.

  • span_id: Identifier of the span entered
  • modkeys: Pressed modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[str, List[str]], None]

on_mouse_leave_span

Called when the mouse pointer leaves a span.

  • span_id: Identifier of the span left
  • modkeys: Pressed modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[str, List[str]], None]

on_mouse_hover_spans

Triggered every time the set of hovered spans changes.

  • span_ids: List of currently hovered span identifiers
  • modkeys: Pressed modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[List[str], List[str]], None]

on_mouse_select

Triggered when the user finishes selecting text with the mouse.

  • ranges: Final list of selected ranges
  • modkeys: Modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[List[Dict[str, int]], List[str]], None]

key

React reconciliation key (not the same as the previous _key props), this should be used to uniquely identify the component instance if there are multiple instances next to each other.

TYPE: Union[str, int]

docs.title: DataWidgetFactory
docs.text:
DataWidgetFactory builds the widgets of a view from a Store. Its widgets read the rows of the Store, save the edits to it, and share the selected rows: selecting a note in a table shows its text in a text widget and its fields in a form. Review entities builds a first view with it.

from metanno import DataRelation, DataWidgetFactory

factory = DataWidgetFactory(
    store, relations=[DataRelation("notes", "entities", on="note_id")]
)

relations links the tables of the Store, here the entities to their note, see Annotate across levels.

docs.title: Widgets
Behavior in the interface
docs.text:
The widgets behave the same way in every view:

  • a checkbox or a choice is saved as soon as it is clicked, a text field when you press Enter or click elsewhere, while Esc, or selecting another row, cancels it
  • when several rows are selected, changing a field changes it for all of them, as one edit
  • Ctrl+Z undoes the last change made in the view and Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes it, with Cmd on a Mac, while inside a text field these keys undo the typing
  • when Python refuses an edit, for instance because someone else changed the same cell, the field shows why. A Metanno tab shows the last refusal under the view, add create_status_bar to views shown in a notebook or a web app
  • the text widget shows the document of the selected row, or with docs_mode="selected" every selected document, and with docs_mode="all" all the documents of the table

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Build tables, forms and annotation views that share a PRET Store.

Widgets created by this factory edit the same data and share row selection. The factory keeps selection separately from the data so navigation does not enter the data undo history.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION data

Existing PRET Store, or initial mapping of row lists and DataFrames

TYPE: Union[Store, Dict[str, Any], Callable[[], Dict]]

sync

Used when creating a Store from initial data. False or None keeps edits in the browser. True synchronizes with Python without saving to disk. A file path also saves edits and lets other Python processes open the same Store

TYPE: Optional[Union[bool, str, PathLike]] DEFAULT: None

relations

Parent and child columns used to filter linked tables

TYPE: Sequence[DataRelation] DEFAULT: ()

read_only

Disable mutations from these widgets without changing notebook access to the Store

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

docs.title: create_table_widget
docs.text: Create a Table widget bound to a store entry. Field metadata is inferred from the underlying data, with optional callbacks for selection changes, hover, and cell content clicks. An imperative handle can be exposed for scrolling and filtering.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION store_key

Key pointing to the list-like store to render.

TYPE: Any

primary_key

Column identifying rows, shared selections store its values. Required for lists of rows, with None a DataFrame table clears its selection when its rows change.

TYPE: str | None

fields

Field metadata used for rendering and editing. Expects:

  • key: Field key.
  • name: Field display name.

  • kind: Field data kind:

    • "text": Plain text.
    • "boolean": Boolean values.
    • "hyperlink": Clickable hyperlink.
    • "select"/"radio"/"autocomplete": Multi choice selection.

  • options: If present, a dropdown/autocomplete will be used with the provided options (can also be a function that takes the selected sample as input and returns options).

  • editable: If True, cells in this column are editable.
  • filterable: If False, no filter control will be rendered.

TYPE: Sequence[FieldSpec]

style

Inline style of the table container, which fills its parent unless these keys override it, eg a fixed height in a notebook output.

TYPE: Dict[str, Any] | None DEFAULT: None

handle

Imperative handle exposing helpers :

  • scroll_to_row_id(row_id): Scroll to the row with the given primary key
  • scroll_to_row_idx(row_idx): Scroll to the specified row index.
  • select_row_id(row_id): Select the row with the given primary key, as a click on it would.
  • set_filter(col, value): Apply a filter on the given column.
  • get_filters(): Retrieve the current filter mapping.
  • clear_filters(): Clear all active filters.
  • set_highlighted(row_ids): Highlight the specified rows by their IDs.
  • get_adjacent_row_id(current_row_id, delta): Retrieve the next/previous row ID within the filtered view, wrapping around.
  • get_adjacent_row_idx(current_row_idx, delta): Retrieve the next/previous row index within the filtered view, wrapping around.

TYPE: RefType[TableWidgetHandle] | None DEFAULT: None

accept_related_filter_keys

Controls whether this table accepts filters broadcast by other views when the factory declares no relation for them, tables linked by a DataRelation follow the selection of their parent instead. True accepts all incoming filters, False accepts none, and a sequence restricts accepted filter keys.

TYPE: bool | Sequence[str] DEFAULT: True

on_selection_change

Called when focus moves inside the table.

  • row_id: Primary key of the focused row.
  • row_idx: Index of the focused row.
  • col: Field key receiving focus.

from metanno import Table

table_state = create_store([
    {"id": "1", "date": "2023-01-01", "text": "Sample text 1", "type": "ENT", "labels": ["ready"]},
    {"id": "2", "date": "2023-01-03", "text": "Sample text 2", "type": "OTHER", "labels": ["ready", "danger"]},
    {"id": "3", "date": "2023-01-05", "text": "Sample text 3", "type": "ENT", "labels": ["blue"]},
    {"id": "4", "date": "2023-01-07", "text": "Sample text 4", "type": "OTHER", "labels": ["bad"]},
    {"id": "5", "date": "2023-01-09", "text": "Sample text 5", "type": "ENT", "labels": []},
    {"id": "6", "date": "2023-01-11", "text": "Sample text 6", "type": "OTHER", "labels": ["custom"]},
    {"id": "7", "date": "2023-01-13", "text": "Sample text 7", "type": "FOO", "labels": ["ready"]},
    {"id": "8", "date": "2023-01-15", "text": "Sample text 8", "type": "FOO2", "labels": ["danger"]},
    {"id": "9", "date": "2023-01-17", "text": "Sample text 9", "type": "FOO3", "labels": ["blue"]},
    {"id": "10", "date": "2023-01-19", "text": "Sample text 10", "type": "ENT", "labels": ["bad"]},
    {"id": "11", "date": "2023-01-21", "text": "Sample text 11", "type": "OTHER", "labels": ["custom"]},
    {"id": "12", "date": "2023-01-23", "text": "Sample text 12", "type": "ENT", "labels": ["ready"]},
    {"id": "13", "date": "2023-01-25", "text": "Sample text 13", "type": "OTHER", "labels": ["danger"]},
    {"id": "14", "date": "2023-01-27", "text": "Sample text 14", "type": "FOO2", "labels": ["blue"]},
    {"id": "15", "date": "2023-01-29", "text": "Sample text 15", "type": "FOO3", "labels": ["bad"]},
])

columns = [
    {"key": "id", "kind": "text", "name": "id", "filterable": True},
    {"key": "date", "kind": "text", "name": "end", "filterable": True},
    {"key": "text", "kind": "text", "name": "text", "filterable": True, "editable": True},
    {"key": "type", "kind": "text", "name": "label", "filterable": True, "editable": True, "choices": ["ENT", "OTHER", "STUFF", "FOO", "FOO2", "FOO3"]},
    {"key": "labels", "kind": "multi-text", "name": "labels", "filterable": True, "editable": True, "choices": ["ready", "danger", "blue", "bad", "custom"]},
]

@component
def MyTable():
    @use_event_callback
    def on_cell_change(row_id, row_idx, col, new_value):
        table_state[row_idx][col] = new_value

    view_state = use_store_snapshot(table_state)
    return Table(
        primary_key="id",
        rows=view_state,
        columns=columns,
        auto_filter=True,
        on_cell_change=on_cell_change,
    )

MyTable()

docs.title: make_dataframe_queries
docs.text:
Load the scope of each factory DataFrame in the browser, the rows shown by all its widgets.

Related tables load as a group, a child scope is filtered by its parent scope, for example the entities of the listed notes. fetchScope queries every scope of the group, then setScope shows them together, so widgets never show new notes with the entities of old ones. Initial loading visits roots before children, querying from a child first finds its parents then loads the remaining branches.

Returns mount, the effect of every factory DataFrame widget, where the first mount loads every group and reloads it when the Store revision changes and the last cleanup stops, and query_from, called by the query button of a table and when a source preview scrolls past its loaded rows.

docs.title: AnnotatedImage
docs.text:
An interactive image viewer that supports drawing, selecting, and styling geometric shapes (polygons, rectangles, points...) as annotations.

Under the hood, we use Konva to render the image and its annotations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from pret import component, create_store, use_store_snapshot, use_event_callback
from metanno import AnnotatedImage
import time

# Reactive store holding the annotation list
img_state = create_store([
    {
        "id": "1",
        "type": "polygon",
        "points": [10, 10, 50, 20],
        "label": "OBJ",
        "style": "primary",
    }
])

# Style preset referenced from the annotation above
img_annotation_styles = {
    "primary": {
        "strokeColor": "red",
        "strokeWidth": 2,
        "fillColor": "rgba(255,0,0,0.5)",
        "labelPosition": "center",
        "align": "center",
        "verticalAlign": "top",
    },
    "secondary": {
        "strokeColor": "blue",
        "strokeWidth": 2,
        "fillColor": "#0000ff80",
        "textColor": "white",
    }
}

@component
def MyImage():
    tracked_state = use_store_snapshot(img_state)

    @use_event_callback
    def on_mouse_select(modkeys, shapes):
        # Toggle 'mouseSelected' flag
        for shp in shapes:
            img_state.append({
                "id": str(time.time()),
                "points": shp["points"],
                "label": "OBJ",
                "style": "primary",
            })

    @use_event_callback
    def on_click(shape_idx, modkeys):
        if shape_idx is None:
            img_state.clear()
        else:
            old_style = img_state[shape_idx].get("style", "primary")
            new_style = "secondary" if old_style == "primary" else "primary"
            img_state[shape_idx]["style"] = new_style

    return AnnotatedImage(
        image="https://picsum.photos/400/300",
        annotations=tracked_state,
        annotation_styles=img_annotation_styles,
        on_mouse_select=on_mouse_select,
        on_click=on_click,
    )

MyImage()

docs.text:
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION annotations

List of annotation objects drawn on top of the image. Each annotation must contain the geometric type and points fields (defining the shape) plus optional metadata such as:

  • id: Optional unique identifier.
  • label: Human-readable text shown next to the shape.
  • style: Key that looks up visual properties in annotation_styles.
  • selected / highlighted / mouseSelected: Booleans used by the component when rendering interaction state.

TYPE: Any

annotation_styles

Named style presets referenced by the style field of an annotation. Each preset may define properties such as stroke color, fill color, opacity, font size, and label alignment, using the following properties:

  • strokeColor (str): Color of the shape's stroke (e.g. "#ff0000").
  • strokeWidth (int): Width of the shape's stroke in pixels.
  • fillColor (str): Background color of the shape (e.g. "#0000ff80").
  • opacity (float): Opacity of the shape's fill (0.0 to 1.0).
  • shape (str): Shape type, e.g. "polygon", "rectangle", "circle", etc.
  • fontSize (int): Font size for the label text.
  • align ("left" | "center" | "right"): Horizontal alignment of the label text.
  • verticalAlign ("top" | "middle" | "bottom"): Vertical alignment of the label text.

TYPE: Any

image

Source URL or base-64 data URI of the image to annotate.

TYPE: str

mouse_selection

Temporary shapes being drawn by the user while the mouse button is held down. Supplied back to on_mouse_select when the gesture ends.

TYPE: Any

Inline CSS-compatible style overrides for the root element of the component.

TYPE: Any

Optional imperative handle that the parent may call (empty for now).

React key for stable reconciliation.

Invoked when the user clicks on an existing shape.

TYPE: Any

Invoked when the component has focus and the user presses a key.

  • key: The key name ("Escape", "Delete" …)

docs.text: The AnnotatedText is a rich text viewer that supports span-level annotations, nested token highlights, and various user event callbacks.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from pret import (
    component,
    create_store,
    use_store_snapshot,
    use_event_callback,
    use_state,
)
from metanno import AnnotatedText
from pret_joy import Button, Box

txt = (
    "Metanno brings annotation components to Pret\n"
    "to build tailored annotation tools."
)

# One span covering the word “Metanno”
spans = create_store(
    [
        {
            "id": f"span-0-7",
            "start": 0,
            "end": 7,
            "label": "OBJ",
            "highlighted": False,
        }
    ]
)

txt_annotation_styles = create_store(
    {
        "OBJ": {
            "color": "red",
            "shape": "underline",
        }
    }
)


@component
def MyText():
    tracked_spans = use_store_snapshot(spans)
    tracked_styles = use_store_snapshot(txt_annotation_styles)

    @use_event_callback
    def handle_select(ranges, modkeys):
        for sp in ranges:
            spans.extend(
                [
                    {
                        "id": f"span-{sp['begin']}-{sp['end']}",
                        "start": sp["begin"],
                        "end": sp["end"],
                        "label": "OBJ",
                    }
                ]
            )

    def on_mouse_enter_span(span_id, modkeys):
        for i, sp in enumerate(spans):
            if sp["id"] == span_id:
                spans[i]["highlighted"] = True

    def on_mouse_leave_span(span_id, modkeys):
        for i, sp in enumerate(spans):
            if sp["id"] == span_id:
                spans[i]["highlighted"] = False

    def on_span_style_change():
        old_style = txt_annotation_styles["OBJ"]["shape"]
        new_style = "box" if old_style == "underline" else "underline"
        txt_annotation_styles["OBJ"]["shape"] = new_style

    return Box(
        Button("Change style", on_click=on_span_style_change),
        Button("Remove annotations", on_click=lambda: spans.clear()),
        AnnotatedText(
            text=txt,
            spans=tracked_spans,
            annotation_styles=tracked_styles,
            label_formatter=lambda span: f"{span['label']} ({span['end'] - span['start']} chars)",
            on_mouse_select=handle_select,
            on_mouse_enter_span=on_mouse_enter_span,
            on_mouse_leave_span=on_mouse_leave_span,
            style={"gridColumn": "1 / -1"},
            begin_key="start",  # Custom field names
        ),
        sx={
            "p": 1,
            "display": "grid",
            "gridTemplateColumns": "repeat(2, auto)",
            "gap": 1,
        },
    )


MyText()

docs.text:
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION text

Raw text content shown in the viewer.

TYPE: str

spans

Span-level annotations over text. Each span must include:

  • begin (or the value of begin_key): Begin character offset (inclusive).
  • end (or the value of end_key): End character offset (exclusive).

and may optionally include:

  • id (or the value of primary_key): Optional unique span identifier.
  • label (or the value of label_key): Category name displayed next to / above the span.
  • style (or the value of style_key): Key referencing annotation_styles.
  • selected (or the value of selected_key): styled as selected by the user.
  • highlighted (or the value of label_key): styled as highlighted by the user.

TYPE: List[Dict[str, Any]]

annotation_styles

Named style presets that control span background color, border, label placement, etc. Each style may define properties such as:

  • color (str): Color of the span. Will be overridden by backgroundColor and borderColor.
  • shape ("underline" | "box"): Visual style of the span.
  • backgroundColor (str): Background color of the span (e.g. "#0000ff80").
  • borderColor (str): Border color of the span (e.g. "#000000").
  • autoNestingLayout (bool): Whether to automatically nest overlapping spans, rather than rendering them on top of each other.

TYPE: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]]

mouse_selection

Current mouse drag selection expressed as character‐offset ranges. Passed to on_mouse_select when the action completes.

TYPE: List[Dict[str, int]]

style

CSS style overrides for the outer element.

TYPE: Dict[str, Any]

handle

Imperative handle for actions that can be performed on the component:

  • scroll_to_line(line_idx: int, behavior: "smooth" | "instant" | "auto"): Scrolls to the given line index.
  • scroll_to_span(span_id: str, behavior: "smooth" | "instant" | "auto"): Scrolls to the given span.
  • clear_current_mouse_selection(): Clears the current mouse selection.

TYPE: Dict[str, Any]

begin_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the begin character offset.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'begin'

end_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the end character offset.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'end'

primary_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the unique span identifier.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'id'

label_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the human-readable label.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'label'

label_formatter

Optional function used to compute each displayed span label from the full span dictionary. When provided, its return value is shown instead of the uppercased value from label_key.

TYPE: Optional[Callable[[Dict[str, Any]], str]] DEFAULT: None

style_key

Name of the field in spans that contains the style key. This key will be used to look up visual properties in annotation_styles. If no style field is provided for a span, the style key will default to label.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'style'

highlighted_key

Name of the field in spans that indicates whether the span is highlighted.

TYPE: str DEFAULT: 'highlighted'

Identifiers of spans styled as highlighted by adding a class to their elements, without tokenizing the text again. Prefer it for fast changing highlights such as hovered spans.

TYPE: Optional[List[str]] DEFAULT: None

on_click_span

Called when the user clicks on a span.

  • span_id: Identifier of the clicked annotation
  • modkeys: Pressed modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[str, List[str]], None]

on_key_press

Called when a key is pressed with focus inside the component.

  • key: Key name
  • ranges: Current selection ranges
  • modkeys: Modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[str, List[Dict[str, int]], List[str]], None]

on_mouse_enter_span

Called when the mouse pointer enters a span.

  • span_id: Identifier of the span entered
  • modkeys: Pressed modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[str, List[str]], None]

on_mouse_leave_span

Called when the mouse pointer leaves a span.

  • span_id: Identifier of the span left
  • modkeys: Pressed modifier keys

TYPE: Callable[[str, List[str]], None]

Triggered every time the set of hovered spans changes.

  • modkeys: Pressed modifier keys

docs.title: Metanno v0
docs.text:
Metanno v0 is a JupyterLab extension for building custom annotation interfaces. It focuses on textual documents with structured entities and aims for modularity, customization, and interactivity. Core features include multi-line and nested span annotations, table-based relational annotations, multiple data types (hyperlinks, text, lists), and an immutable state that can be synchronized between the frontend and backend. The project compiles Python app classes to JavaScript using Transcrypt, enabling fast, browser-side execution while keeping Python code on the kernel side. To create an app, the user must modify one of the apps in recipes/*.py, and handle state management using a huge Redux-style reducer in select_state.

Last items in the v0 changelog:

  • Almost complete typescript conversion
  • Added column filters
  • Customizable undo/redo logic
  • Editable span annotations from a table view
  • Accessible return value of a Python call from front end (async calls)

In this first tutorial, you open a small pandas table in a Metanno tab, mark some notes as reviewed, and read your annotations back in Python. It takes about five minutes and needs no configuration.

Before you start

Install Metanno as described in Installation, then open a notebook in JupyterLab.

Run this cell, which puts three notes in a Store, the object Python and Metanno share:

import pandas as pd
from pret import DataFrame, create_store

from metanno import view_opener

notes = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"note_id": 1, "text": "Follow-up on Monday", "reviewed": False},
        {"note_id": 2, "text": "No further treatment", "reviewed": False},
        {"note_id": 3, "text": "Follow-up in 3 months", "reviewed": False},
    ]
)
store = create_store({"notes": DataFrame(notes)}, sync=True)
view_opener(store)

The cell shows an opener:

Click Open with Metanno: a tab opens beside your notebook, with the table on the left and the Selected rows panel on the right. The menu next to the button chooses how to display the data: table for now, and your own views once you write some, like note_tnm above.

Try the table before going further:

  • type follow in the box under the text header to keep the matching notes
  • click the ⋮ button of a column header to sort by that column
  • select a row to see its fields in Selected rows
What can I type in a filter box? Filter text Keeps rows where the column follow contains follow, or equals it for numbers and booleans = 1, != 1, < 1, >= 1 compares with the value in (1, 2) equals one of the values starts with follow, ends with up starts or ends with the text is null, is not null is missing or present

docs.title: Make it editable
docs.text:
This first tab is a preview: you can look, but not edit. To annotate, save the Store to a file and open the saved copy:

from pret import save_store

saved = save_store(store, "review.pret")
view_opener(saved)

Click the new Open with Metanno. In this tab, double-click the text of note 1, change it to Follow-up on Tuesday and press Enter, then tick the reviewed box of notes 1 and 3.

There is no save button: each edit is written to review.pret as soon as you make it.

What is review.pret?

A SQLite database holding your table and the history of its edits, which also lets you undo with Ctrl+Z. Pret's Inside a Store file explains what it contains. save_store never overwrites a file: if you run the cell again, use load_store("review.pret") instead.

docs.title: Read your annotations in Python
docs.text:
Back in the notebook, the saved Store already holds your edits:

saved["notes"].materialize().to_pandas()
note_id text reviewed 0 1 Follow-up on Tuesday True 1 2 No further treatment False 2 3 Follow-up in 3 months True

It also works the other way around. Run this cell while watching the tab:

saved["notes"].update(identity={"note_id": 2}, values={"reviewed": True})

The box of note 2 gets ticked: Python and the tab edit the same data. The notes pandas table you started from is left unchanged.

docs.title: Come back later
docs.text:
Close the tab, or even restart the kernel. To continue, run in any notebook of the same folder:

from pret import load_store

from metanno import view_opener

view_opener(load_store("review.pret"))

Your edits are all there, and new ones keep being saved to the same file.

Find it in the sidebar

Files saved in the views/stores folder, at the root of the JupyterLab file browser, are listed in the Metanno sidebar, so you can reopen them without a notebook. The next tutorial shows that sidebar.

docs.title: Annotate across levels
docs.text:
Some decisions are not about a note but about a patient: is this patient eligible for the study, given all their notes? Annotators then need to read every note of a patient before answering. In this tutorial, you add a patients table above the notes, and a view where selecting a patient shows their notes, and selecting a note its entities.

Before you start

Follow Design your view first: this tutorial adds patients to its oncology.pret file.

docs.title: Add the patients
docs.text:
Build one row per patient from the notes, with the number of notes and an eligible column to fill:

from pret import DataFrame, load_store

store = load_store("views/stores/oncology.pret")
notes = store["notes"].materialize().to_pandas()
patients = notes.groupby("patient_id", as_index=False).agg(note_count=("note_id", "count"))
store["patients"] = DataFrame(patients.assign(eligible=False))
store["patients"].materialize().to_pandas()
patient_id note_count eligible 0 10 2 False 1 12 2 False

The file now holds three tables, linked by two columns: patient_id between patients and notes, note_id between notes and entities.

docs.title: Write the view
docs.text:
%%writefile views/recipes/patient_review.py
from pret_joy import Stack
from pret_simple_dock import Layout, Panel

from metanno import DataRelation, DataWidgetFactory

LABELS = {
    "tumeur": {"name": "Tumeur", "color": "rgb(255,200,206)", "shortcut": "t"},
    "tnm": {"name": "TNM", "color": "rgb(210,236,247)", "shortcut": "n"},
}


def main(store):
"""
    Decide on each patient while reading their notes and entities
    """
    # One relation per link between two tables. The notes table shows the
    # notes of every listed patient (working_set), the text the entities
    # of the selected note (selection, the default)
    factory = DataWidgetFactory(
        store,
        relations=[
            DataRelation("patients", "notes", on="patient_id", load="working_set"),
            DataRelation("notes", "entities", on="note_id"),
        ],
    )

    # The patient level decision
    patients = factory.create_table_widget(
        store_key="patients",
        primary_key="patient_id",
        fields=[
            {"key": "patient_id", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "note_count", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "eligible", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
        ],
        style={"height": "100%"},
    )

    # Notes of the listed patients, starting with those of the selected
    # patient only, a checkbox above the table shows them all
    notes = factory.create_table_widget(
        store_key="notes",
        primary_key="note_id",
        fields=[
            {"key": "note_id", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "patient_id", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "department", "kind": "text"},
        ],
        follow_parent_selection=True,
        parent_row_name="patient",
        style={"height": "100%"},
    )

    # Text of the selected note with its entities
    text, toolbar = factory.create_text_widget(
        store_text_key="notes",
        store_spans_key="entities",
        text_key="text",
        text_primary_key="note_id",
        spans_primary_key="entity_id",
        fields=[{"key": "label", "kind": "select", "editable": True, "options": list(LABELS)}],
        labels=LABELS,
    )

    # Patients above their notes on the left, the text on the right
    return Layout(
        Panel(patients, key="Patients"),
        Panel(notes, key="Notes"),
        Panel(Stack(toolbar, text, spacing=1), key="Text"),
        default_config={
            "kind": "row",
            "children": [
                {"kind": "column", "size": 35, "children": [{"tabs": ["Patients"]}, {"tabs": ["Notes"]}]},
                {"tabs": ["Text"], "size": 65},
            ],
        },
    )

A DataRelation links a parent table to a child table through a column they share, and decides which child rows the child widgets show:

load The child table shows Use it when selection, the default the rows of the selected parent row only you work on one parent at a time, such as the entities of a note working_set the rows of every parent row listed, after its filters you also compare parents, such as the notes of all eligible patients

With working_set, follow_parent_selection=True starts the child table on the selected parent row only, with a Selected patient only checkbox to switch to the whole working set.

docs.title: Open it
docs.text:
from metanno import view_opener

view_opener(store, view="patient_review")

Then go through the patients:

  • select patient 12: notes 4 and 5 are listed, select note 4 to read it
  • untick Selected patient only to see the notes of every patient, then type oncologie under department to keep the oncology notes only
  • tick eligible for the patients you would include
Small data as nested lists

For a few hundred records built in Python, a Store can also hold nested lists of dictionaries, without DataFrames, such as {"patients": [{"patient_id": 10, "notes": [...]}]}. Widgets then point to the nested level with a dotted path, store_key="patients.notes", and need no DataRelation. Prefer DataFrames for data coming from a database: they are what Prepare annotation produces, and they stay fast on large tables.

docs.title: Browse a database
docs.text:
In this tutorial, you connect a small database to Metanno and browse its tables from the JupyterLab sidebar, without writing a query. The same steps work with your own database, whether it is a DuckDB file, PostgreSQL, Spark or Trino.

Before you start

Follow Installation, including the metanno-explorer kernel. From now on, create the notebooks of these tutorials at the root of the JupyterLab file browser, where Metanno keeps its configuration and your views. This tutorial uses DuckDB, install its driver in the same environment:

pip install 'ibis-framework[duckdb]'

docs.title: Create a sample database
docs.text:
Run this cell in a notebook. It writes a few clinical notes to clinic.duckdb, next to the notebook, in French like the notes EDS-NLP pre-annotates in a later tutorial:

from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import pandas as pd

rows = [
    (1, 10, "oncologie", "2026-01-05", "Cancer du sein, stade pT2N0M0."),
    (2, 10, "oncologie", "2026-02-10", "Pas de complication."),
    (3, 11, "cardiologie", "2026-01-20", "Fibrillation atriale."),
    (4, 12, "oncologie", "2026-03-02", "Tumeur cT3N1M0, pas de métastase."),
    (5, 12, "radiologie", "2026-03-15", "Mammographie sans lésion."),
    (6, 13, "cardiologie", "2026-04-01", "Insuffisance cardiaque."),
]
columns = ["note_id", "patient_id", "department", "note_date", "text"]
notes = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=columns)
notes["note_date"] = pd.to_datetime(notes["note_date"])
path = Path("clinic.duckdb").resolve()
with duckdb.connect(str(path)) as connection:
    connection.register("new_notes", notes)
    connection.execute("CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE notes AS SELECT * FROM new_notes")
print(path)

Keep the printed path, you need it in the next step.

docs.title: Tell Metanno where it is
docs.text:
Click the Metanno icon in the left sidebar of JupyterLab, the two overlapping windows shown on the right. The panel is empty for now: Metanno only lists the sources declared in its configuration file.

Click Open configuration at the top of the panel. It opens metanno.yaml in an editor, created at the root of the file browser the first time, replace its content with the following, using the path printed above:

connections:
clinic:
url: duckdb:///home/you/clinic.duckdb
sources:
clinic:
connection: clinic

Save the file, then click the reload button ↻ next to Open configuration.

connections says how to reach a database, and sources lists what the panel shows. Here a single source uses the clinic connection, but a connection can serve several sources, for instance one per schema of the same database.

docs.title: Explore a table
docs.text:
Under Explore, a clinic source now appears. Expand it and click notes: the table opens in a tab, with the selected note on the right like in Annotate a table.

This tab reads the database directly, without copying it. To keep things fast on large tables, it shows a preview of at most 500 rows, in no particular order, and edits are disabled since they would change your database.

The boxes under the column headers filter the rows of this preview only. To search the whole table, type your filters in these boxes, then click Apply source filters above the table: Metanno sends them to the database and shows the matching rows. For instance, type oncologie under department and apply it to the source.

What else is in the tab toolbar? Button What it does View menu Shows the same rows with another view, table or one of your own Copy code Writes notebook code for the current query, the next tutorial uses it Refresh Reloads the table, after the database changed or its connection failed Fullscreen Fills the browser tab with the view, its URL reopens the same table

Right-click a table in the panel and choose Open in new tab to keep the current tab.

docs.title: What the panel lists
docs.text:
The panel has two parts:

  • Explore lists your sources and their tables, and the saved views you will create in Design your view
  • Annotations lists the files saved in the views/stores folder, next to metanno.yaml, such as the ones you will create in the next tutorial. Click one to reopen it, without opening its notebook
Other kinds of sources

Besides the tables of a database, a source can list the Parquet or Delta datasets of a folder, or the tables of one schema of a larger database. A connection can also be opened by your own Python function, for instance to read credentials:

connections:
warehouse:
factory: project_connections:connect
kwargs:
database: /data/warehouse.duckdb
sources:
oncology:
connection: warehouse
database: oncology
exports:
connection: warehouse
kind: files
format: parquet
uri: /data/exports
preview:
rows: 1000
  • catalog and database select the catalogue and the database, or schema, holding the tables of a source
  • kind: files lists the datasets in the uri folder, local or on HDFS and S3 through a Spark connection
  • factory names a function, here connect in a project_connections.py file next to metanno.yaml, which returns an Ibis connection or a context manager giving one, and receives the kwargs
  • preview.rows changes the 500 rows shown by source tabs
from contextlib import contextmanager

import ibis


@contextmanager
def connect(database):
    backend = ibis.duckdb.connect(database)
    try:
        yield backend
    finally:
        backend.disconnect()

Connections open the first time one of their tables is shown. Install the Ibis driver of each one, such as ibis-framework[postgres], in the environment of the metanno-explorer kernel.

docs.text:
Work in progress

This tutorial is being written. It will show how to write widgets that read the selected rows of the factory and save edits like the built-in ones, for instance a summary of the selected patient or a timeline of their notes. The helpers these widgets need are not public yet.

The factory widgets cover tables, texts, forms and PDFs, but a view can hold any Pret component next to them. A common case is an annotation guide, kept in a panel beside the text so annotators check the rules without leaving the tab.

docs.title: Add a guide panel
docs.text:
In views/recipes/oncology_review.py from Design your view, write the guide as a component:

from pret_joy import Typography


def guide():
"""
    Show the annotation rules of the project
    """
    return Stack(
        Typography("Annotation guide", level="title-md"),
        Typography("Tumeur: any tumor mention, including negated ones."),
        Typography("TNM: the complete stage, such as cT3N1M0."),
        Typography("Site: the organ of the primary tumor."),
        spacing=1,
        sx={"p": 1},
    )

then add it as a panel of the layout, stacked as a tab with the note questions:

     layout = Layout(
         Panel(notes, key="Notes"),
         Panel(text, key="Text", header=header),
         Panel(Stack(form, Divider(), toolbar, spacing=1), key="Note"),
+        Panel(guide(), key="Guide"),
        Panel(entities, key="Entities"),
         default_config={
             ...
-                        {"tabs": ["Note"], "size": 50},
+                        {"tabs": ["Note", "Guide"], "size": 50},

Click the reload button of the tab toolbar: a Guide tab now sits next to Note.

Pret components are written in Python like React components, the Pret tutorials show how to give them a state and make them interactive.

docs.title: Design your view
docs.text:
Annotators review faster with an interface fitted to their task: the text large in the middle, the questions about the whole note next to it, and keyboard shortcuts for the labels they use most. In this tutorial, you turn the review_entities view into such an interface, and see what else DataWidgetFactory widgets can show.

Before you start

Follow Review entities first: this tutorial builds on its oncology.pret file and its view.

docs.title: Add questions about each note
docs.text:
Besides its entities, annotators should tell for each note the site of the cancer, and mark it as reviewed. Add these two columns to the notes of the file:

from pret import DataFrame, load_store

store = load_store("views/stores/oncology.pret")
notes = store["notes"].materialize().to_pandas()
store["notes"] = DataFrame(notes.assign(reviewed=False, site=None).astype({"site": "string"}))

site starts empty, and its string type tells Metanno which values it will hold.

docs.title: Write the interface
docs.text:
The new view arranges four panels: the notes on the left, the text in the middle, and on the right a form with the note questions above the entities of the note:

%%writefile views/recipes/oncology_review.py
from pret_joy import Divider, Stack
from pret_simple_dock import Layout, Panel

from metanno import DataRelation, DataWidgetFactory

# Name, color and keyboard shortcut of each entity label
LABELS = {
    "tumeur": {"name": "Tumeur", "color": "rgb(255,200,206)", "shortcut": "t"},
    "tnm": {"name": "TNM", "color": "rgb(210,236,247)", "shortcut": "n"},
}
# Choices offered for the cancer site of a note
SITES = ["sein", "poumon", "autre"]


def main(store):
"""
    Review notes with their entities, in panels annotators can rearrange
    """
    factory = DataWidgetFactory(
        store,
        relations=[DataRelation("notes", "entities", on="note_id")],
    )

    # Notes to review, with a checkbox to mark them as reviewed
    notes = factory.create_table_widget(
        store_key="notes",
        primary_key="note_id",
        fields=[
            {"key": "note_id", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "department", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "reviewed", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
        ],
        style={"height": "100%"},
    )

    # Questions about the selected note, with buttons to move to the
    # previous or next note
    form = factory.create_form_widget(
        store_key="notes",
        primary_key="note_id",
        fields=[
            {"key": "site", "kind": "radio", "editable": True, "options": SITES},
            {"key": "reviewed", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
        ],
        add_navigation_buttons=True,
    )

    # Text of the selected note, its label toolbar, and a header showing
    # the ID of the note above the text
    text, toolbar = factory.create_text_widget(
        store_text_key="notes",
        store_spans_key="entities",
        text_key="text",
        text_primary_key="note_id",
        spans_primary_key="entity_id",
        fields=[
            {"key": "label", "kind": "select", "editable": True, "options": list(LABELS)},
            {"key": "negated", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
        ],
        labels=LABELS,
    )
    header = factory.create_selected_field_view(
        store_key="notes", shown_key="note_id", fallback="Note"
    )

    # Entities of the selected note
    entities = factory.create_table_widget(
        store_key="entities",
        primary_key="entity_id",
        fields=[
            {"key": "text", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "label", "kind": "select", "editable": True, "options": list(LABELS)},
            {"key": "negated", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
            {"key": "checked", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
        ],
        style={"height": "100%"},
    )

    # Panels can be resized, dragged and stacked as tabs. default_config
    # gives their first arrangement, as rows and columns of tab groups
    layout = Layout(
        Panel(notes, key="Notes"),
        Panel(text, key="Text", header=header),
        Panel(Stack(form, Divider(), toolbar, spacing=1), key="Note"),
        Panel(entities, key="Entities"),
        default_config={
            "kind": "row",
            "children": [
                {"tabs": ["Notes"], "size": 20},
                {"tabs": ["Text"], "size": 50},
                {
                    "kind": "column",
                    "size": 30,
                    "children": [
                        {"tabs": ["Note"], "size": 50},
                        {"tabs": ["Entities"], "size": 50},
                    ],
                },
            ],
        },
    )
    # The status bar under the panels reports rejected edits and the
    # connection to Python
    return Stack(layout, factory.create_status_bar(), style={"height": "100%"})

As in review_entities, Metanno calls main with the Store of the file it opens, the same file the first cell loaded as store, and shows what main returns. Compared to that view, three things are new:

  • a form, create_form_widget, shows the fields of the selected note, with ← Previous and Next → buttons to go through the notes
  • a shortcut per label: select some text and press T to add a tumor, without reaching for the toolbar
  • a Layout of Panels, from pret_simple_dock, the Pret version of react-simple-dock, instead of a vertical Stack

docs.title: Open it
docs.text:
from metanno import view_opener

view_opener(store, view="oncology_review")

The menu of the opener lists both of your views, oncology_review and review_entities, and opens the one you choose. Try the new interface:

  • drag the title of the Entities panel onto Notes to stack them as tabs, or resize the panels by dragging their borders
  • select poumon for note 4 in the form, tick reviewed, then click Next →
  • in the text, select a word and press T, click an entity and press Backspace to delete it, and press Left or Right to change notes

Opening the file from the sidebar now uses oncology_review, the last view you opened it with.

docs.title: Choose how each field is shown
docs.text:
Each entry of fields picks a column, and kind picks how its values are shown and edited:

kind Shows Edited with text the value as text a text box boolean a checkbox a click select the value a dropdown of options radio the value radio buttons, in forms autocomplete the value a searchable list of options, for long lists hyperlink a link not editable

editable allows edits, and filterable, True by default, shows the filter box of a table column. options can also be a function of the row, to offer different choices for each note:

def site_options(note):
"""
    Offer the breast site first for radiology notes, mostly mammographies
    """
    return ["sein", "autre"] if note["department"] == "radiologie" else SITES


{"key": "site", "kind": "radio", "editable": True, "options": site_options}
Working faster in tables
  • click the ⋮ button of a column header to sort by that column, pin it to the left, or show and hide columns
  • drag a column header onto another one to move it
  • Ctrl+C copies the selected cells, Ctrl+Shift+C the selected rows with the column names
  • Ctrl+Z undoes the last change made in the view, Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes it

On a Mac, use Cmd instead of Ctrl.

Use your view on database tables

The view menu of a source tab in the sidebar also lists your views. To open a view on several database tables at once, save a file such as views/oncology.yml, which then appears under Explore in the sidebar. This one assumes your database also holds an entities table:

recipe: review_entities
tables:
notes:
source: clinic
table: notes
entities:
source: clinic
table: entities

Each entry of tables becomes a table of the Store your view receives, read from the database without copying it.

docs.title: Prepare the next notes for your questions
docs.text:
You added reviewed and site by hand at the beginning of this tutorial. For the next notes you pick, let Prepare annotation add them: a view can define annotation_setup_code, a function returning code that the copied cell runs before saving the notes. The source tab must be able to show this view, so it can only use the notes table, like this view of the note questions:

%%writefile views/recipes/note_questions.py
from pret_simple_dock import Layout, Panel

from metanno import DataWidgetFactory

# Choices offered for the cancer site of a note
SITES = ["sein", "poumon", "autre"]


def main(store):
"""
    Answer questions about each note while reading it
    """
    factory = DataWidgetFactory(store)
    notes = factory.create_table_widget(
        store_key="notes",
        primary_key="note_id",
        fields=[
            {"key": "note_id", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "department", "kind": "text"},
            {"key": "reviewed", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
        ],
        style={"height": "100%"},
    )
    # Without store_spans_key, the text widget only shows the text
    text, _ = factory.create_text_widget(
        store_text_key="notes", text_key="text", text_primary_key="note_id"
    )
    questions = factory.create_form_widget(
        store_key="notes",
        primary_key="note_id",
        fields=[
            {"key": "site", "kind": "radio", "editable": True, "options": SITES},
            {"key": "reviewed", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
        ],
        add_navigation_buttons=True,
    )
    return Layout(
        Panel(notes, key="Notes"),
        Panel(text, key="Text"),
        Panel(questions, key="Questions"),
        default_config={
            "kind": "row",
            "children": [
                {"tabs": ["Notes"], "size": 25},
                {"tabs": ["Text"], "size": 50},
                {"tabs": ["Questions"], "size": 25},
            ],
        },
    )


def annotation_setup_code(parameters):
"""
    Add the columns of the note questions to the notes copied by Prepare annotation
    """
    return 'tables["notes"] = tables["notes"].with_columns(reviewed=False, site="")'

Open the notes table of the clinic source in the sidebar, choose note_questions in the view menu of the tab, then click Copy code → Prepare annotation. The copied cell now adds the two columns before saving the notes:

tables = {
    'notes': DataFrame(notes),
}

tables["notes"] = tables["notes"].with_columns(reviewed=False, site="")

and the saved file opens with note_questions, ready for your annotators.

annotation_setup_code receives the parameters of the view: the arguments of main besides store, which a saved view file gives under parameters: and view_opener under parameters=. They let the setup code follow the options of the view. note_questions has none, so parameters is empty and the function ignores it.

docs.title: Outside JupyterLab
docs.text:
The Metanno tab is convenient while you prepare a project, but annotators do not always use JupyterLab, and a view sometimes belongs in a notebook next to an analysis. In this tutorial, you show the view of Review entities below a notebook cell, then serve it as a web app.

Before you start

Follow Review entities first: this tutorial reuses its oncology.pret file and its review_entities view.

docs.title: In a notebook output
docs.text:
A view is a function returning a Pret component, so calling it at the end of a cell shows the view below the cell:

import sys

from pret import load_store

sys.path.insert(0, "views/recipes")
from review_entities import main

store = load_store("views/stores/oncology.pret")
main(store)

The output is the same interface as the tab, editing the same file, so an edit made here also shows in the Metanno tab.

From an output to a tab

Right-click a Pret output to open it in a new browser tab, or to detach it into its own JupyterLab panel, see From notebook to app.

docs.title: As a web app
docs.text:
To give annotators a link instead of a notebook, serve the view with Pret. Save this script as app.py, at the root of the file browser:

import sys

from pret import load_store, run

sys.path.insert(0, "views/recipes")
from review_entities import main

if __name__ == "__main__":
    store = load_store("views/stores/oncology.pret")
    run(main(store), port=5000)

then start it from a terminal, in that folder:

python app.py

and open http://localhost:5000. Edits are saved to oncology.pret, like in the tab, and the notebook, the tab and the app show each other's edits since they all use the same file.

Who can reach the app

run only listens to your own machine by default. run(..., host="0.0.0.0") makes the app reachable from other machines, without any login: anyone who can reach the port can read and edit the annotations. Only do it on a network you trust, or behind the access control of your institution.

docs.title: Pick documents
docs.text:
An annotation project rarely covers a whole database: you first select the documents worth annotating, such as the notes of one department over a year. In this tutorial, you turn a query on the sample database into an annotation file holding an editable copy of the selected notes, without writing the query yourself.

Before you start

Follow Browse a database first: this tutorial starts from its clinic source.

docs.title: Filter the notes
docs.text: In the Metanno sidebar, open the notes table of the clinic source. Type oncologie in the box under department, then click Apply source filters: the tab now shows the oncology notes only.

docs.title: Copy the code
docs.text:
Click Copy code in the tab toolbar, then Prepare annotation, and paste the copied code in a notebook cell. It connects to the database, queries the oncology notes, saves them to an annotation file and opens it. Its comments describe each step, and the paths are the ones of your own machine.

Before running it, adapt two lines to your project. Add the radiology notes to the cohort, so that breast imaging reports are reviewed with the oncology notes, and give the file a meaningful name:

-    .filter(_['department'] == 'oncologie')
+    .filter(_['department'].isin(['oncologie', 'radiologie']))
...
-destination = Path('/home/you/views') / 'stores' / 'annotation.pret'
+destination = Path('/home/you/views') / 'stores' / 'oncology.pret'

With these changes, the code reads as below, with your own paths instead of /home/you. Paste your version in the empty cell under it:

from pathlib import Path

import ibis
from ibis import _

from pret import DataFrame, create_store, load_store, save_store
from metanno import view_opener


config_path = '/home/you'

# Connections of metanno.yaml, rerun this cell if a connection is lost
clinic = ibis.connect('duckdb:///home/you/clinic.duckdb')

# Queries select source records, change the filters and limits for your cohort
notes = (
    clinic.table('notes')
    .filter(_['department'].isin(['oncologie', 'radiologie']))
    .limit(500)
)

# Tables maps the prepared data to the Store keys expected by the view recipe
tables = {
    'notes': DataFrame(notes),
}

# Parameters are keyword arguments for the view recipe, they do not change the source queries
parameters = {}

# Save editable copies of the query results and added fields, without changing the source database
destination = Path('/home/you/views') / 'stores' / 'oncology.pret'
# Annotation views copy every table into the page so filters and edits apply at once, up to 50 MB.
# The options are saved with the Store and used again when it is reopened
options = {'dataframe_sync': 'full', 'dataframe_max_bytes': 50 * 1024 * 1024}
save_store(create_store(tables, sync=True), destination, metadata={
    'view': 'table', 'parameters': parameters, 'config_path': config_path, **options,
})
store = load_store(destination, **options)
view_opener(store)

Run it, then click Open with Metanno: the four selected notes open in an editable tab. oncology.pret also appears under Annotations in the sidebar, where you or a colleague can reopen it later.

A copy, not the database

The annotation file holds a copy of the selected notes: edits go to oncology.pret, and your database is never modified. The copy is limited to the 500 first rows of the query, raise .limit(500) when your cohort is larger, and keep in mind that the whole selection is loaded in the annotation tab.

Only exploring?

Copy code → Customize query writes the same query without saving anything, to continue exploring the data in Python, for instance with pandas or Ibis.

docs.title: Pre-annotate
docs.text:
Finding every tumor mention by hand is slow, while checking a mention that is already highlighted is quick. In this tutorial, you run an EDS-NLP pipeline on the notes you picked, and save the entities it finds, tumors and TNM stages, next to the notes, ready to be reviewed.

Before you start

Follow Pick documents first: this tutorial adds entities to its oncology.pret file. Install EDS-NLP in your notebook environment:

pip install edsnlp

docs.title: Build the pipeline
docs.text:
The pipeline splits the notes into sentences, matches a few tumor terms, detects TNM stages, then flags the entities that are negated, such as the metastasis in "pas de métastase":

import edsnlp
import edsnlp.pipes as eds

nlp = edsnlp.blank("eds")
nlp.add_pipe(eds.sentences())
nlp.add_pipe(eds.normalizer())
nlp.add_pipe(eds.matcher(terms={"tumeur": ["cancer", "tumeur", "métastase"]}, attr="NORM"))
nlp.add_pipe(eds.tnm())
nlp.add_pipe(eds.negation())
nlp

Pipeline(lang=eds, pipes={
  "sentences": eds.sentences,
  "normalizer": eds.normalizer,
  "matcher": eds.matcher,
  "tnm": eds.tnm,
  "negation": eds.negation
})

Try it on a sentence before running it on your notes:

doc = nlp("Tumeur cT3N1M0, pas de métastase.")
[(ent.text, ent.label_, ent._.negation) for ent in doc.ents]

[('Tumeur', 'tumeur', False), ('cT3N1M0', 'tnm', False), ('métastase', 'tumeur', True)]

docs.title: Pre-annotate the notes
docs.text:
Open the annotation file and read its notes. EDS-NLP then streams them through the pipeline and returns one row per entity, which you save in a new entities table of the file:

from pret import DataFrame, load_store

store = load_store("views/stores/oncology.pret")
notes = store["notes"].materialize().to_pandas()

entities = (
    edsnlp.data.from_pandas(
        notes.rename(columns={"text": "note_text"}),
        converter="omop",
        doc_attributes=["note_id"],
        nlp=nlp,
    )
    .map_pipeline(nlp)
    .to_pandas(converter="ents", span_attributes={"negation": "negated"})
    .rename(columns={"start": "begin", "lexical_variant": "text"})
    .drop(columns="span_type")
    .assign(
        entity_id=lambda df: df["note_id"].astype(str) + "-" + df["begin"].astype(str),
        checked=False,
    )
)
store["entities"] = DataFrame(entities)
store["entities"].materialize().to_pandas()
note_id begin end label text negated entity_id checked 0 1 0 6 tumeur Cancer False 1-0 False 1 1 22 29 tnm pT2N0M0 False 1-22 False 2 4 0 6 tumeur Tumeur False 4-0 False 3 4 7 14 tnm cT3N1M0 False 4-7 False 4 4 23 32 tumeur métastase True 4-23 False

from_pandas reads the notes, keeping their note_id, map_pipeline runs the pipeline on them, by batches for large corpora, and to_pandas returns their entities, with negated from the negation step. Each row points to its note with note_id, and to its characters with begin, included, and end, excluded. checked is the column annotators will tick once they reviewed an entity.

Saved at once

Like any change to a saved Store, the new table is written to oncology.pret as soon as you add it, with no save step. It is also an editable copy: changing a row in Metanno never reruns the pipeline.
